title: 9/10/2026 | Clare Nelson | LTRS | Email to DOE Secretary Wright on September 10, 2026. Subject: Pause Texas 765-kV Projects Pending Federal Bulk-Power Security Review. References Executive Order, “Declaring a National Emergency to Secure the United States Bulk-Power System."

documents.text:
=== Email to DOE Secretary Wright.pdf ===
Email sent to DOE Secretary Wright on September 10, 2026




Subject: Urgent Request: Pause Texas 765-kV Projects Pending Federal Bulk-Power Security
Review

CC: DOE Office of Cybersecurity; Energy Security, and Emergency Response
(CESER); Texas Cyber Command; PUCT Chairman Gleeson; Texas Attorney General Paxton
(via website); Texas Governor Greg Abbott (via website)



Dear Secretary Wright,

I am writing to ask for your immediate help regarding the massive buildout of new 765-kV
transmission infrastructure underway in Texas.

President Trump’s August 26, 2026 Executive Order, “Declaring a National Emergency to Secure
the United States Bulk-Power System,” raises fundamental national-security questions that, in my
view, are reason enough to stop or pause these 765-kV projects until the federal government
completes the security work directed by the President.

Texas is moving in the opposite direction, at breakneck speed. The Texas Legislature cut the
Certificate of Convenience and Necessity (CCN) process for these transmission projects from
approximately one year to just 180 days. Billions of dollars of infrastructure could therefore be
approved before DOE has completed the risk assessments, vendor identification, and implementing
measures contemplated by the new Executive Order.

For the proposed 765-kV system, Texas landowners deserve answers to basic national-security
questions:

   •   Where will the transformers, breakers, relays, PLCs, RTUs, intelligent electronic devices,
       software, and firmware be manufactured or developed?
   •   Who will have remote access to that equipment and software?
   •   Do the procurement plans of Oncor, LCRA, AEP and other utilities include equipment,
       components, or software originating from entities that could ultimately be designated as
       Covered Foreign Entities?
   •   Have ERCOT and the Public Utility Commission of Texas evaluated the STEP procurement
       and cybersecurity architecture against the new federal national-security standard?
   •   Why should billions of dollars of new bulk-power infrastructure be approved or
       constructed before DOE identifies high-risk equipment and vendors and issues the
       rules necessary to implement the President’s order?

During the Texas Senate Business & Commerce Committee Hearing on April 1, 2026, members
were told that compliance with the Lone Star Infrastructure Protection Act, SB 2116 for supply chain
security, may rely on supplier attestations. For infrastructure this critical, self-attestation is not
 enough. We require independent verification, not supplier attestations for a project of this magnitude
and scope. And Texas security is tied directly to US national security.

These security issues are particularly urgent because the utilities have enormous financial incentives
to keep these projects moving. Sempra, the indirect majority owner of Oncor, has made Texas
utility investment a major component of its growth strategy. Oncor stands to earn a regulated
return on billions of dollars of new transmission investment. Financial incentives should not be
allowed to outrun national security.

Once this infrastructure is approved, easements are condemned, equipment is ordered, and
construction begins, it becomes enormously difficult and expensive to reverse course. Security
needs to be addressed before these systems are built, not after billions of dollars have been
committed.

I respectfully ask DOE to consider whether Texas and other states should pause approval,
procurement, or construction of major new 765-kV bulk-power facilities until DOE completes
the actions required by the August 26 Executive Order, particularly those concerning foreign
adversaries, covered equipment, supply-chain vulnerabilities, remote access, and software and
firmware security. At the Texas House Committee on State Affairs Hearing on August 19, 2026,
Oncor stated it has started procurement for long lead time components. On an earnings call in Q3
2025, Sempra refers to Oncor's Midlothian Supply Center, south of Dallas, Texas.

I am an affected Texas landowner and a retired business executive and cybersecurity professional. I
have testified before the Texas Legislature and the Public Utility Commission about the
security implications of this enormous transmission buildout, and submitted that testimony
in the PUCT Docket 59475 as items 6494 and 6500, available
here: https://interchange.puc.texas.gov/search/filings/?ControlNumber=59475&ItemMatch=0&
SortBy=ItemNumber&SortOrder=Ascending&Page=4. We need federal help. The state process
is moving far faster than the national-security review now ordered by the President.

The central question is simple: Why are we rushing to build a new generation of critical
bulk-power infrastructure before we know whether the equipment, vendors, software,
firmware, and remote-access arrangements meet the security standards the federal
government is now developing?

    •   We should be building modular, micro-grid architecture that can operate when one
        portion goes down.
    •   Instead, 765-kV is being forced on Texas. This is technology from before 1969, when
        it first went operational in the US in Ohio. It is very old technology, and hard to
        secure.

I would welcome the opportunity to provide DOE with additional information about the Texas 765-kV
projects and the accelerated approval process.

Thank you for your attention to this urgent matter.

Sincerely,

Clare Nelson
 Affected Texas Landowner
Retired Business Executive and Cybersecurity Professional

Attachment: August 26, 2026 Executive Order 14420 – 765-kV Security Issues




Sent with Proton Mail secure email.
